instructions.task: At the end of this step, could an agent tell from the completion criterion whether the step is done or not done?

criteria.true: It names things the agent can check: a result produced, slots filled, items each matched to a source, a decision recorded, a list compared. A criterion that points at returns the step's body spells out counts as naming them. So does one stated as what a later reader or caller can do with the step's result, when the body names what that result holds: the agent checks the result for it, as 'the next phase can start without asking for a missing input' is checked against the inputs the body lists.
criteria.false: It names a state of mind or an activity with nothing to check, such as 'understanding reached', 'the code is reviewed' or 'context gathered'.

instructions.task: Can the criterion be met only by doing the work the step asks for, rather than by a thin or empty result?

criteria.true: It can't be written without the step's real work: it names what had to be opened, read, compared or run, or ties each item it requires to its evidence, as 'name every caller of the changed function and say which ones break' does. A criterion that requires the return or result the step's body spells out item by item demands that legwork too, because those items can't be produced without the work. So does one that requires every item of the step's subject to carry the properties the body names, as 'each endpoint has its owner, its auth rule and its error shape' does; one that requires the artifact the step produces, in the place the body sets and holding what the body says it holds; or one that requires the statement or decision the step exists to make, at the moment the body sets, when making it is the step's whole work.
criteria.false: A thin or empty result meets it: 'produce a change list' is met by a list of nothing, and 'note any issues' by 'none' without looking.

no.finding: Completion criterion doesn't let the agent tell done from not done.
Completion criterion can be met without the step's legwork.

instructions.task: What kind of text is this?

criteria.guidance: Guidance: an instruction or a standard that tells the agent what to do, or what not to do. That includes a limit a result must keep, and an item without its own verb in a list whose lead-in instructs, such as a field to capture, a value to choose or a condition to check, which carries the lead-in's instruction.
criteria.other: Something else: an example, a fact, a definition, a quotation, rationale, or a statement of what a role, file or skill owns.

instructions.task: Does the guidance give a positive target, an action to take or what a good result looks like, rather than only naming what to avoid?

criteria.true: It names an action or a target, even when it also forbids something, or sends the agent to another skill and says what to bring back from it. A standard that states the property a good result has, and then rules out what breaks it, names the target. A limit names its target too, the side of the bound a good result stays on, as 'a function over 80 lines fails review' does. So does an item without its own verb in a list whose lead-in instructs: a value to choose, with the condition that selects it, names the action of choosing it, and a check item, even one worded 'no …', names the state the check confirms, as 'no failing tests' does in a list of checks to run.
criteria.false: It only names what to avoid or not do, and leaves the agent to guess the target, as 'Don't skip tests' or 'Never guess an API' do. A full sentence that bans something without saying what to do instead names only what to avoid, as 'configs carry no secrets' does when nothing says where secrets go.

no.finding: Guidance names only what to avoid; give the action or result to aim for.
